oneSentence: A machine-learning model pretrained at large scale on broad data can be adapted for many tasks without training a new model from scratch.
plainExplanation:
A foundation model is a machine-learning model trained first on a very large and varied collection of data. That first stage is often called pretraining. The aim is to build a general starting point that can later be adapted to many tasks.

What goes in at the start is usually large-scale data, such as text, images, audio or a mix of these. During training, the system adjusts many numerical settings, often called parameters, so that it becomes better at predicting patterns in that data. What comes out is not a finished service by itself, but a reusable base that others can fine-tune, instruct, connect to tools or place inside an application.

This is different from a model built for just one narrow job, such as detecting a specific defect in one factory or forecasting one type of demand. A foundation model is intended to be general-purpose within the kinds of data it was trained on. It may support summarising, classification, drafting, search assistance or other tasks after adaptation, but that does not mean it is equally good or safe for all of them.

People often confuse foundation models with large language models. Many large language models are foundation models, but not all foundation models work only with language. Some handle images, speech or several data types together. The exact boundary is still debated, so the term is useful but not perfectly settled.

everydayAnalogy.title: A musician learning a new set list
everydayAnalogy.story: A musician who has spent years learning rhythm, harmony and many styles does not begin again from the first lesson whenever a new performance is booked. That broad training helps them learn a jazz set, accompany a choir or play at a school concert. Each performance still requires the right music, rehearsal and adjustment to the audience. In the same way, a foundation model supplies broad capabilities that can be adapted for different tasks, but it is not ready for every task without further work and checking.

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A library catalogue is a human-made index with explicit entries. A foundation model does not store knowledge in neat labelled cards. It learns statistical patterns through numerical adjustment, and it can generate fluent but wrong output. Also, a catalogue mostly helps you find existing books, while a foundation model can also produce new text, images or other outputs.

visual.title: How a foundation model becomes useful for many tasks
visual.learningObjective: After viewing, the reader should be able to explain that one broadly pretrained model can be adapted into several task-specific systems.
visual.description: Show one left-to-right flow with four boxes. Large mixed data goes into pretraining, which produces a base model. From that single model, three branches lead to different adapted uses such as summarising, image labelling and search assistance. Read from left to right, then down the branches.

steps.label: Large varied data
steps.explanation: Training starts with a very large dataset, often containing text, images, audio or several types together.

steps.label: Pretraining
steps.explanation: The system adjusts many parameters to learn broad statistical patterns in the data.

steps.explanation: The output is a reusable starting model, not yet tailored to one organisation's exact task.

visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram is a left-to-right flow. First, a box labelled 'Large datasets' shows that training begins with broad data such as text, images and audio. An arrow leads to 'Pretraining', where the model learns statistical patterns by adjusting parameters. Another arrow leads to a central box labelled 'Foundation model or base model', showing the reusable result of that first training stage. From there, three arrows branch outward to 'summarise documents', 'classify images' and 'search assistant'. The main message is that one broadly pretrained model can be adapted for several different tasks instead of training a separate model from zero for each task.

workedExample.scenario: A reporting officer at a regional bureau is asked to pilot an assistant that produces first drafts of a weekly monitoring report from approved public material in English, Arabic and French.
workedExample.input: A broadly pretrained multilingual model, an approved collection of public reports and human-reviewed examples showing the required structure and terminology.
process: The officer starts with the pretrained model rather than commissioning a model trained from scratch for weekly reporting.
The pilot connects the model to the approved document collection and gives it instructions based on the established monitoring report format.
Reviewers test the assistant on material withheld from development, checking factual accuracy, omissions, citations and performance in each language.
The assistant is limited to first drafts. The reporting officer verifies every claim against the source material before the report enters clearance.
workedExample.result: One broadly pretrained model has been adapted to a specific reporting task without being rebuilt from zero. The same model could support other applications, but each would require separate configuration, evaluation, controls and human review.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: At a country office town hall, a staff member asks whether the proposed drafting assistant is a different AI model from the one demonstrated for document search. The knowledge management officer has to answer before the discussion moves to the next agenda item.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: Both applications may use the same foundation model. Its broad pretraining provides a reusable starting point, while prompting, retrieval or further tuning adapts it for drafting or search. Each application still needs its own design, testing and oversight.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Reuse does not make every use appropriate. The officer should not enter personal, protection-sensitive, security-sensitive or other confidential material into a tool that has not been approved for it. Each application also requires checks for accuracy, access controls, language performance and fitness for purpose.

whyItMatters: Non-specialists hear this term in procurement, governance and risk discussions because it changes how AI systems are built and bought. Instead of commissioning a separate model for each use, organisations may start from one broadly trained model and adapt it. That can reduce time and cost, but it also changes the questions leaders should ask: what data was used in pretraining, what limits are known, what tasks has it actually been evaluated for, who controls the weights or access, and what safeguards exist for privacy, bias, safety and accountability. The label also matters because not every impressive model is a suitable foundation for public-sector work.

An ICT governance board reviewing an AI pilot
An inter-agency working group discussing shared digital tools
A front-office briefing before clearance of an AI concept note

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A foundation model can do any task well straight away.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Broad pretraining gives a useful starting point, not guaranteed competence. Performance varies by task, language, domain and context. A model may need further adaptation, testing and safeguards before it is reliable enough for real use.

Many chatbots are built on foundation models, but the terms are not the same. A chatbot is an application or interface. A foundation model is the underlying broadly pretrained model, which may support chat, search, image tasks or other uses.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If a model is called foundational, its output is authoritative.
commonMisconceptions.correction: The term describes how the model was trained and reused, not whether each answer is correct. Outputs still need verification because models can reflect gaps in data, produce errors and perform unevenly across topics or languages.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: It is a large starter model trained on broad data so people can adapt it for many different jobs later.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: A foundation model is a machine-learning model, usually with many parameters, pretrained on large-scale and diverse data to learn general-purpose representations or predictive capabilities that transfer across downstream tasks. After pretraining, it can be adapted through fine-tuning or instruction tuning, or applied through prompting, retrieval, tool use or other methods. The term usually implies broad reuse across applications, but definitions differ: some authors restrict it to models with substantial scale and wide task transfer, while others use it more loosely for any broadly pretrained base model. It is related to, but not identical with, large language models, multimodal models or frontier models.

keyTakeaway: A foundation model is a reusable starting point for many AI applications, not a finished product. Every application still needs adaptation, testing, safeguards and oversight.

quickCheck.question: Which description best fits a foundation model?
options: A fixed rule-based system written for one exact workflow
A broadly pretrained model that can be adapted for many later tasks
Any AI system that produces human-like conversation
The most powerful model available anywhere at a given time
quickCheck.explanation: The key idea is broad pretraining plus later adaptation for multiple downstream uses. A rule-based system is different, a chatbot is just one possible application, and 'most powerful available' refers more to frontier model discussions than to the definition of foundation model.

contested: The term has no single universally accepted boundary. Different authors use it more narrowly or more broadly, especially when distinguishing it from large language models, multimodal models and frontier models.

issues.problem: The definition is too broad. A model that is merely broadly trained and reusable could be an ordinary pretrained model. The defining idea also includes pretraining at scale on broad data.
issues.fix: A machine-learning model pretrained at large scale on broad data can be adapted for many tasks without training a new model from scratch.

issues.problem: The limitation says a foundation model can generate new content and fluent but wrong output. That is not true of every foundation model and blurs the term into generative AI. Some foundation models are used only to produce representations or classifications.
issues.fix: A library catalogue is a human-made index with explicit entries. A foundation model does not store knowledge in neat labelled cards. It learns statistical patterns through numerical adjustment. Some foundation models can generate fluent but wrong output. Also, a catalogue mostly helps you find existing books, while some foundation models can produce new content.

issues.problem: Both fields incorrectly present evaluation, retrieval and tool use as ways of adapting the model. Evaluation measures a system. Retrieval and tool use usually change the surrounding application rather than the model's trained parameters. Prompting changes how the model is used, not the model itself.
issues.fix: In the technical explanation, replace the methods sentence with: "After pretraining, it can be adapted through fine-tuning or instruction tuning, or applied through prompting, retrieval, tool use or other methods." In the visual step, use: "The starting model can be fine-tuned or prompted, and combined with tools for different uses. Each use needs separate evaluation."

issues.problem: The label "Foundation model / base model" presents the terms as synonyms. A foundation model can serve as a base, but "base model" is a broader and context-dependent label that does not by itself mean foundation model.
issues.fix: Label the central box "Foundation model" and add the note "reusable base". Make the same change in the accessibility description.

issues.problem: The process never uses the 50,000 approved documents, while the result adds keyword suggestion and retrieval even though the team adapted and tested only summarisation. No arithmetic result is stated to verify: 50,000, 2,000 and 300 are dataset counts, not operands in a claimed calculation.
issues.fix: Change the input to: "A pretrained multilingual text model and 2,000 human-reviewed examples of good summaries." Change the result to: "The adapted model can produce first-draft summaries across several languages, but any additional use, such as keyword suggestion or retrieval, would need separate implementation, evaluation and oversight."
